title: 22. Interview: HTTP
summary: Interview Q&A for HTTP — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 HTTP interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What does it mean that HTTP is "stateless," and how do real applications build sessions on top of it?
**Answer:** HTTP is stateless at the protocol level: each request carries all the context the server needs to handle it, and the server is not required to remember anything about previous requests. This is what makes HTTP horizontally scalable — any instance can handle any request because there's no per-connection server-side state in the spec. Real applications build sessions on top using cookies: the server returns a `Set-Cookie: session_id=xyz` header on the first response, the client echoes it back as `Cookie:` on subsequent requests, and the server looks up `xyz` in a shared store (Redis, a database) to recover session state. The trade-off is that the session store becomes a dependency: if Redis is down, no one can log in. An alternative is JWT (JSON Web Tokens), which encodes session state directly in the cookie, signed by the server — stateless at the server, but harder to revoke. The HTTP/REST community generally favors statelessness because it maximizes horizontal scalability.
**Visual:**
```
req1:  POST /login  -> server: Set-Cookie: sid=abc
req2:  GET /profile Cookie: sid=abc  -> server: lookup abc in Redis
req3:  GET /orders  Cookie: sid=abc  -> server: lookup abc in Redis
(no server-side per-connection state required by HTTP itself)
```

### Q2. What is the difference between HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing?
**Answer:** HTTP/1.1 keep-alive lets a single TCP connection carry multiple requests, but they must be sequential — the client sends request 1, waits for the response, then sends request 2. This avoids the TCP/TLS handshake cost per request but still suffers head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer: a slow request blocks all later requests on the same connection. Browsers work around this by opening 6 parallel TCP connections per origin. HTTP/2 multiplexing eliminates the HTTP-level blocking: many logical streams (each identified by a stream ID) share one TCP connection, and the server can respond in any order; the client reassembles streams by ID. So a slow response on stream 1 doesn't block stream 2. The trade-off is that HTTP/2 still has TCP-level head-of-line blocking: a lost TCP packet stalls all streams on that connection until retransmission. HTTP/3 fixes this by running streams over QUIC, where each stream has independent loss recovery.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive:    req1 -> resp1 -> req2 -> resp2   (sequential)
HTTP/2 multiplexing:    req1, req2, req3 --(parallel streams on 1 TCP)-->
                        <-- resp2, resp1, resp3 (any order)
HTTP/3 (QUIC):          same as H2, but lost packet stalls only 1 stream
```

### Q3. What is the difference between idempotent and safe HTTP methods, and why does it matter for retries?
**Answer:** A method is "safe" if it has no side effects (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) — calling it must not change server state. A method is "idempotent" if calling it N times has the same effect as calling it once (GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD). POST is neither safe nor idempotent — each POST may create a new resource, so a retried POST after a network timeout could create duplicate orders. This matters enormously for retry logic: clients can safely retry idempotent methods on transient failures (5xx, timeouts), but must not blindly retry POST. The standard fix is the `Idempotency-Key` header (popularized by Stripe): the client generates a unique key per logical operation, sends it on the POST, and the server deduplicates by key — if it sees the same key again, it returns the cached response instead of creating a new resource. PUT and DELETE are naturally idempotent: `PUT /users/42` with the same body always results in the same final state, and `DELETE /users/42` twice has the same effect as once.
**Visual:**
```
Safe:       GET, HEAD, OPTIONS            (no side effects)
Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD        (N calls == 1 call)
Neither:    POST, PATCH                   (use Idempotency-Key)

POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: abc123  -> 201 Created (charge_001)
POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: abc123  -> 201 Created (charge_001)  [cached]
POST /charges  Idempotency-Key: def456  -> 201 Created (charge_002)  [new]
```

### Q4. Explain the role of the common HTTP status codes 200, 201, 204, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504.
**Answer:** 200 OK is the default success. 201 Created is success with a new resource (POST that creates), typically with a `Location` header. 204 No Content is success with no body (DELETE, PUT with no echo). 301 Moved Permanently tells the client to update its bookmark and use the new URL. 304 Not Modified is the conditional GET response when the client's `If-None-Match`/`If-Modified-Since` matches — the server skips the body, saving bandwidth. 400 Bad Request means the client sent malformed input (invalid JSON, missing field). 401 Unauthorized means the client is not authenticated. 403 Forbidden means the client is authenticated but lacks permission. 404 Not Found means the resource doesn't exist. 429 Too Many Requests means rate limited, with a `Retry-After` header. 500 Internal Server Error is a generic server bug. 502 Bad Gateway is a proxy that got an invalid response from upstream. 503 Service Unavailable is the server temporarily down (with `Retry-After`). 504 Gateway Timeout is the proxy that didn't get a response in time. Choosing the right code is high-signal: 401 vs 403 vs 404 distinguishes auth problems from permission problems from missing resources.
**Visual:**
```
2xx OK            200, 201, 204
3xx Redirect      301, 302, 304
4xx Client fault  400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429
5xx Server fault  500, 502, 503, 504

401 vs 403 vs 404 decision tree:
  no auth header?                       -> 401 Unauthorized
  auth ok but lacks permission?         -> 403 Forbidden
  auth ok, permitted, but resource?     -> 404 Not Found
```

### Q5. What is content negotiation, and how does it enable one API to serve multiple clients?
**Answer:** Content negotiation is the mechanism by which client and server agree on the representation of a resource. The client sends `Accept: application/json` (or `application/protobuf`, `text/html`, `image/webp`) and `Accept-Language: en-US`, and the server picks a representation it can produce, returning it with `Content-Type: application/json`. This is how a single `/products/42` endpoint can serve HTML to a browser, JSON to a mobile app, and Protobuf to an internal microservice. There are two flavors: server-driven (the client sends `Accept` headers, server decides) and agent-driven (server returns a 300 Multiple Choices with links, client picks). Server-driven is far more common. A real-world example: GitHub's API serves JSON by default but supports `Accept: application/vnd.github.v3.diff` to get a diff representation of the same PR. The trade-off is that content negotiation couples the client and server to MIME-type strings and forces the server to maintain multiple serializers. Some teams sidestep this by using separate endpoints (`/products/42.json`, `/products/42.html`), which is simpler but less RESTful.
**Visual:**
```
GET /products/42
Accept: application/json      <-- client prefers JSON
Accept-Language: en-US

<- 200 OK
   Content-Type: application/json
   Content-Language: en-US
   {"id":42,"name":"..."}
```

### Q6. Why did HTTP/3 replace TCP with QUIC, and what problem does it actually solve?
**Answer:** HTTP/2 multiplexed many streams over a single TCP connection, which solved HTTP-level head-of-line blocking but exposed TCP-level head-of-line blocking: if one TCP packet is lost, the kernel holds back all bytes (across all streams) until retransmission succeeds, because TCP's in-order guarantee applies to the byte stream, not to logical streams. QUIC rebuilds TCP's reliability on top of UDP, but gives each stream its own sequence number space and its own loss recovery — a lost packet on stream 5 only stalls stream 5, while streams 1, 3, 7 keep flowing. QUIC also combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes into a single 1-RTT exchange (or 0-RTT for resumed sessions), saving a full RTT over HTTPS-on-TCP. And QUIC survives IP address changes (mobile network handoff from Wi-Fi to LTE) via connection IDs, which TCP cannot do because TCP uses the 4-tuple as the connection identifier. Cloudflare, Google, and Facebook all deployed HTTP/3 broadly, reporting 10–30% latency improvements on mobile. The trade-off: QUIC's userspace implementation has higher CPU cost than kernel TCP, and some networks (corporate firewalls, oppressive regimes) block UDP.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP/2 over TCP:  one packet lost -> ALL streams stall until retransmit
HTTP/3 over QUIC: one packet lost -> ONLY the affected stream stalls

Mobile handoff (Wi-Fi -> LTE):
  TCP: 4-tuple changes -> connection dies -> app must reconnect
  QUIC: connection ID stays -> connection survives -> no user-visible glitch
```

### Q7. What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
**Answer:** 401 means "I don't know who you are" — the client failed to authenticate. The response should include a `WWW-Authenticate` header describing how to authenticate (e.g., `Bearer`). 403 means "I know who you are, but you can't do this" — the client authenticated successfully but lacks authorization for the specific resource or action. The distinction matters because it tells the client what to fix: 401 means "go get a token" (redirect to login), 403 means "ask an admin for permission" (no point retrying with the same token). A common mistake is returning 401 when the user is authenticated but lacks permission — that confuses clients and security tools, which interpret 401 as "the token is invalid, refresh it." Another mistake is returning 404 instead of 403 to hide the existence of a resource — this is sometimes intentional (don't leak that the resource exists), but it breaks REST semantics and should be documented. The decision tree is simple: no/invalid auth header → 401; valid auth but no permission → 403; valid auth and permission but resource missing → 404.
**Visual:**
```
missing/invalid Authorization header?       -> 401 + WWW-Authenticate
authenticated but role lacks permission?     -> 403 Forbidden
authenticated, permitted, but resource gone? -> 404 Not Found
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your REST API creates orders via POST. Users complain of duplicate charges after network timeouts. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** POST is not idempotent, so a retried POST creates a second order. The fix is the `Idempotency-Key` header, popularized by Stripe. The client generates a UUID per logical operation (e.g., per "place order" button click) and sends it as `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` on the POST. The server stores the key in Redis with a TTL of 24 hours and the response (status, body, headers) it produced. On a retry with the same key, the server looks up the cached response and returns it instead of creating a new order. If the first request is still in flight, the server returns 409 Conflict (or holds the second request until the first completes) to prevent concurrent duplicates. The key must be generated client-side and unique per logical operation, not per HTTP request — the client must reuse the same key across retries of the same logical operation. Stripe's docs are the canonical reference; AWS API Gateway and many payment processors support the same pattern. The trade-off is the Redis dependency and 24-hour storage cost, which is negligible compared to the cost of duplicate charges.
**Visual:**
```
client retries POST /orders after timeout:

POST /orders  Idempotency-Key: abc  body={...}
  (network timeout, but server actually created order #1)

POST /orders  Idempotency-Key: abc  body={...}   <-- retry, SAME key
  -> server: lookup "abc" in Redis
  -> found! return cached 201 Created {"id":1,...}
  (no duplicate order created)
```

### Q2. A paginated list endpoint returns 1000 items in 8 seconds; clients complain. How would you restructure the HTTP API?
**Answer:** The first problem is probably that the server is doing too much work in one request (N+1 queries, no DB index). But from an HTTP perspective, the API should be paginated with cursor-based pagination, not offset pagination. Offset (`?page=5&size=20`) forces the DB to scan and skip 80 rows, which is O(N); cursor (`?after=cursor_xyz&limit=20`) uses an indexed WHERE clause, which is O(limit). The response should include a `next` link (RFC 5988 / RFC 8288 `Link` header) so the client knows how to fetch the next page without constructing URLs. The response should also send `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60` so the same page can be cached briefly. If the list is large and the client needs all of it, offer an async export endpoint that returns 202 Accepted with a `Location` header pointing at the eventual download URL — the client polls until 200 OK. Finally, enable gzip or Brotli compression (`Content-Encoding: gzip`) — JSON compresses 5–10×, which on mobile networks is the single biggest latency win.
**Visual:**
```
Bad:   GET /items?page=5&size=20      (DB scans 100 rows, skips 80)
Good:  GET /items?after=xyz&limit=20  (DB uses index, O(20) rows)
       200 OK
       Link: <...?after=abc>; rel="next"
       Cache-Control: private, max-age=60
       Content-Encoding: gzip
```

### Q3. Your mobile app's first request takes 2 seconds; subsequent requests take 100 ms. What HTTP-layer optimizations would you apply?
**Answer:** The gap is handshake cost. First request pays DNS (1 RTT), TCP SYN/SYN-ACK (1 RTT), TLS 1.2 (2 RTT) or TLS 1.3 (1 RTT), plus the HTTP request itself (1 RTT). On a 200-ms mobile RTT that's 5×200 = 1 second of setup, plus slow-start ramp. Subsequent requests on a warm keep-alive connection pay only 1 RTT. The optimizations: (1) enable HTTP keep-alive on the client and set a generous idle timeout (5–10 minutes) so connections stay warm; (2) upgrade to HTTP/2 so the client multiplexes many requests over one warm connection; (3) use TLS 1.3 (1 RTT handshake) and enable session resumption (0-RTT for returning clients); (4) consider HTTP/3 over QUIC, which combines transport + TLS into 1 RTT (or 0-RTT) and survives mobile network handoffs; (5) use `<link rel=preconnect>` (web) or a startup warm-up call (mobile) to start the handshake before the user's first real request; (6) pre-resolve DNS at app launch. Combined, these can take first-request latency from 2 seconds to 400 ms on mobile.
**Visual:**
```
Cold HTTPS request on 200ms mobile RTT:
DNS 200 + TCP 200 + TLS1.2 400 + HTTP 200 = 1000ms setup
+ slow-start ramp adds 200-500ms
=> ~2s

After fixes (HTTP/2 + TLS1.3 + warm):
TCP+TLS = 200ms (1 RTT, reused)
HTTP req = 200ms (1 RTT)
=> 400ms
```

### Q4. You are designing a webhook delivery system. What HTTP semantics matter most for correctness?
**Answer:** Three things: idempotency, retries, and status-code interpretation. Webhooks are typically POST (non-idempotent), so each webhook must carry a unique event ID, and the receiver must deduplicate by ID — a delivered-but-acknowledged-late webhook will be retried, and the receiver must handle the duplicate gracefully. Retries: the sender should retry on 5xx and on timeouts, with exponential backoff (e.g., Stripe retries up to 16 times over 3 days). The sender must NOT retry on 4xx (the receiver rejected it as malformed — retrying won't help). The receiver should respond 2xx quickly (within 5 seconds) and process the event asynchronously; if it takes longer, the sender's HTTP timeout fires and it retries, creating duplicates. The `Idempotency-Key` header should carry the event ID. Finally, the sender should sign the body (HMAC) with a header like `Stripe-Signature` so the receiver can verify authenticity — anyone can send a POST to a webhook URL. Real-world: Stripe, GitHub, and Slack all follow this pattern; GitHub uses HMAC SHA-256 in `X-Hub-Signature-256`.
**Visual:**
```
Sender -> Receiver:
  POST /webhook
  Idempotency-Key: evt_123
  X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hmac>
  body: {"event":"order.created","id":"evt_123"}

Receiver: verify HMAC, dedupe evt_123, return 200 OK fast, process async.
Sender:   retry on 5xx/timeout with backoff; do NOT retry on 4xx.
```

### Q5. A CDN cache is serving stale data after a deploy. How do HTTP caching headers fix this?
**Answer:** The relevant headers are `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, and `Vary`. `Cache-Control: max-age=60` tells the CDN to serve the cached response for 60 seconds without revalidating. After max-age, the CDN sends a conditional GET with `If-None-Match: <etag>` or `If-Modified-Since: <date>`. If the origin says the content hasn't changed, it returns 304 Not Modified with no body — saving bandwidth but confirming the cache is still valid. If the origin has new content, it returns 200 with the new body and a new ETag. `Vary: Accept-Encoding` tells the CDN to cache separately per encoding (gzip vs br) so a Brotli-capable client doesn't get served a gzip response. To force a cache refresh after a deploy, you can either (a) version the URL (`/app.v2.js` instead of `/app.js`) so the new URL has no cache, or (b) use a short max-age with revalidation (`max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=86400`) so changes propagate within 30 seconds. Netflix uses short max-age on manifest URLs (10–30 seconds) so bitrate switches propagate fast, but long max-age on video segments (hours) since they're immutable.
**Visual:**
```
GET /api/products  (CDN cache expired)
If-None-Match: "abc123"

<- 304 Not Modified          (no body, cache confirmed valid)
   ETag: "abc123"

OR

<- 200 OK                    (new content)
   ETag: "def456"
   Cache-Control: max-age=60
   body: ...
```

### Q6. You are migrating a service from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2. What pitfalls should you watch for?
**Answer:** HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, which is great for throughput but introduces subtle pitfalls. First, a single slow request can fill the TCP send buffer and stall other streams if the server doesn't enforce per-stream flow control — this is "request-level head-of-line blocking" reborn at the L4 layer. Second, the connection pool size on the client must shrink: a client that opened 6 HTTP/1.1 connections per origin should now open 1 HTTP/2 connection, but most HTTP clients default to keeping 6. Third, header compression (HPACK) is stateful, so a connection that has been open for hours accumulates a large HPACK table — memory leak risk on long-lived connections. Fourth, HTTP/2 server push was a feature that mostly failed in practice (browsers can't cancel pushed responses cleanly) and was removed in HTTP/3 — don't rely on it. Fifth, some intermediaries (corporate proxies, older CDNs) don't support HTTP/2 and will downgrade to HTTP/1.1, breaking assumptions. Finally, observability tooling built for HTTP/1.1 (one stream per connection) needs upgrading — you now need per-stream tracing. Test with `h2load` or `nghttp` before flipping the default.
**Visual:**
```
HTTP/1.1: 6 TCP conns x 1 stream  = 6 parallel requests
HTTP/2:   1 TCP conn x N streams   = 100+ parallel requests
                                  ^-- one slow stream can fill TCP buffer
                                      and stall others unless per-stream
                                      flow control is enforced
```

### Q7. A client receives intermittent 502 Bad Gateway from your service behind a load balancer. What does 502 mean and how do you debug it?
**Answer:** 502 Bad Gateway is an L7 error returned by a proxy (the load balancer) when it got an invalid response from the upstream server — typically the upstream closed the connection without responding, or sent a malformed HTTP response. The intermittent pattern suggests some backends are healthy and some are not. Debug steps: (1) check LB logs for which backend got the 502 — usually the LB records the upstream IP; (2) check that backend's logs for the same timestamp — did it crash, OOM, or hit a request timeout? (3) check the LB's health check endpoint — if the health check uses `/healthz` but the service is alive on `/`, the LB might be sending traffic to an instance that's actually unhealthy; (4) check the LB's configured timeout — if the backend takes 30s to respond but the LB has a 10s timeout, you'll get 502 (or 504 Gateway Timeout depending on the LB). A common root cause is the backend's `Keep-Alive` timeout being shorter than the LB's connection reuse timeout, so the LB sends a request on a connection the backend has just closed. Fix by aligning the timeouts: backend keep-alive > LB reuse timeout.
**Visual:**
```
Client --HTTPS--> LB --HTTP--> backend_1 (crashed)  => 502
Client --HTTPS--> LB --HTTP--> backend_2 (healthy)  => 200

Root causes to check:
  - backend crash/OOM
  - LB health check vs backend reality mismatch
  - backend keep-alive timeout < LB reuse timeout (closed conn reused)
  - backend response > LB upstream timeout  (often 504, sometimes 502)
```
